projects.rationale: Activist Handbook is community-owned, open-contribution, addresses structural barriers to democratic participation, is partially open source with a self-hosting pathway, and is explicitly designed for grassroots empowerment rather than institutional incumbents.

Adhocracy+ advances participatory democracy with open source, self-hostable technology and public/grant funding, but falls short on community ownership and anti-extraction innovation due to single-organization governance and a primary service focus for institutions rather than marginalized communities.

AISafety.info is an expert-curated educational platform with partial open source and open contribution, but lacks meaningful community ownership, does not enable technological sovereignty or self-hosting, and primarily serves professional and research audiences rather than centering participatory democracy or marginalised communities.

Alaveteli strongly advances participatory democracy and technological sovereignty by enabling citizens to run their own open-source FOI platforms, is governed by a nonprofit with grant funding (not VC), and empowers marginalized users to challenge state opacity, though its governance model is not explicitly user-owned.

Aleph is open source and serves investigative journalists and civil society, but its governance is not community-owned, its funding is heavily reliant on state actors with editorial risks, and evidence of participatory/anti-extractive design is limited in the dossier.

AlgorithmWatch advances algorithmic accountability and serves marginalized communities affected by algorithmic discrimination, but the dossier provides insufficient evidence of community ownership, participatory governance, or strong technological sovereignty/self-hosting beyond partial open source, so it scores moderately for challenging power structures but lacks the deeper structural transformation Gamithra prioritizes.

All Our Ideas demonstrates strong alignment with participatory democracy and community governance, is open source and self-hostable, operates on a nonprofit model, and centers citizen input, but lacks explicit evidence of deep structural anti-extraction innovation or advanced privacy-by-design features in the dossier.

The Responsible Tech Guide 2025 is a curated publication managed by a nonprofit editorial team without community governance, open-source self-hosting, or participatory ownership, and primarily serves professional audiences rather than directly empowering marginalized communities.

Anna's Archive advances open access and technological sovereignty via open source and a grassroots, donation-funded model, but lacks documented community governance and transparency, with an individual governance model and unclear participatory mechanisms.

Landlord Tech Watch is a grassroots, open source, grant/donation-funded project serving tenants and housing advocates, directly challenging extractive proptech by producing critical data and educational materials, though the dossier lacks detailed evidence about participatory governance beyond being a project of a larger org.

Aragon partially enables community governance through token-holder voting and open-source contributions, but its VC-backed LLC structure, incomplete open source, and focus on protocol/DAO users rather than marginalized communities limit its alignment with participatory, anti-extractive, and sovereignty principles.

arXiv advances open access and free knowledge sharing, but its governance is institutionally anchored rather than community-owned, self-hosting is only partially supported, and its primary beneficiaries are academics rather than marginalized communities.

projects.abstain_reason: The dossier provides only a high-level description of a theoretical governance framework without implementation details, evidence of community governance, self-hosting, anti-extraction design, or privacy/data ethics, making it impossible to meaningfully assess the constitutional criteria.
projects.rationale: As an evaluator, I must abstain due to insufficient dossier evidence on real-world governance, sovereignty, anti-extraction, or privacy practices.

Atlas of Surveillance advances participatory documentation of police tech and supports advocacy for marginalized communities, but community governance is limited to contributor review by EFF staff rather than genuine user ownership or control, and self-hosting is only partially enabled.

While the toolkit is open source, supports investigative and citizen journalists, and is nonprofit/grant-funded, there is insufficient evidence of meaningful community governance, self-hosting infrastructure, or explicit anti-extraction design beyond openness, so it lands as a useful civic resource but not a structurally transformative or community-owned project.

While the project serves marginalized communities and addresses poverty, it lacks community ownership, offers no technological sovereignty or self-hosting, and primarily optimizes access to existing welfare systems without challenging structural causes of exclusion.

While Kagi SlopStop offers a community-driven reporting feature and addresses information quality, it is for-profit, lacks evidence of user or community ownership, is only partially open source, and appears dependent on a proprietary platform, thus falling short on technological sovereignty and anti-extraction innovation.

Channel.org is open source, nonprofit, and aims to foster participatory democracy, but lacks evidence of community/user governance, documented self-hosting paths, or explicit anti-extraction design details, warranting a middling score.

The project is a grant-funded report serving professional users in the charity sector with no evidence of community ownership, self-hosting, or structural anti-extraction innovation, and limited civic or participatory features.

Martus is a free, open source, grant-funded tool supporting human rights activists globally, with strong alignment to technological sovereignty and anti-extraction values, but there is insufficient evidence of community ownership or participatory governance, and the project's maintenance and privacy assurances are undermined by discontinued support.

While Mastodon C supports open data and civic tech for institutional users, it lacks community ownership, is structured as an LLC with internal governance, offers only partial open source/self-hosting, and does not demonstrate anti-extractive or participatory innovation for marginalized communities.

meet.coop exemplifies community ownership through its cooperative, member-democratic governance, provides surveillance-free video conferencing on cooperatively owned and partially open-source infrastructure, prioritises privacy and digital rights, and is explicitly structured to serve activists, progressive organizations, and marginalized communities rather than institutional incumbents.

While the project is open source and provides civic data access for citizens, it lacks community ownership, participatory governance, structural anti-extraction innovation, and explicit privacy-by-design features, serving primarily as an academic database rather than a tool for transformative participatory democracy.

MP Watch is a centralized advocacy platform with no evidence of community ownership, self-hosting, or participatory governance, and while it serves civic and climate goals, it lacks anti-extraction design and privacy-by-design features per the dossier.

While MyActionCenter supports participatory democracy and advocacy, it is a proprietary, for-profit tool with no community ownership, no open source or self-hosting, and is dependent on a commercial platform (NationBuilder), thus failing on community governance, technological sovereignty, and anti-extraction criteria.

projects.abstain_reason: The dossier lacks sufficient evidence regarding the project's community ownership/governance model, self-hosting capability, and anti-extraction innovation design, making it impossible to score according to the evaluative constitution.
projects.rationale: Key details on governance, technological sovereignty, and structural change orientation are missing from the dossier, so I must abstain rather than speculate.

GOV.UK Notify is a government-run, centrally controlled notification platform serving public sector agencies rather than citizens or marginalized communities, with only partial open source and no evidence of community governance, technological sovereignty for users, or structural anti-extraction design.

While Objector.ai provides citizens with tools to participate in planning objections and amplifies advocacy, it lacks community ownership, is not open source or self-hostable, and operates as a for-profit LLC with no evidence of participatory governance or anti-extraction innovation beyond improved access.

While Open Contracting Partnership advances public procurement transparency and partially open sources its tools, there is insufficient evidence of community governance, full technological sovereignty, or explicit anti-extraction design, with its primary beneficiaries being institutional actors rather than marginalized communities.

OpenCRVS is open source and grant-funded, enabling some technological sovereignty and public benefit, but its governance and primary users are state institutions rather than communities, and there is insufficient evidence of participatory or anti-extractive design beyond service delivery.

OpenOrigins is a VC-backed, proprietary platform with closed governance and no community ownership, lacking self-hosting or open source options, and while it addresses disinformation, it does so through extractive, centralized means rather than participatory or structurally transformative models.

Open Ownership advances beneficial ownership transparency for anti-corruption and accountability, but the dossier shows it primarily serves governments and institutions rather than directly empowering communities, lacks evidence of participatory governance or full technological sovereignty, and does not demonstrate a structural anti-extraction or community ownership model.

OpenSanctions provides partial open source infrastructure for important civic data, but its governance is not community-owned, its primary users are institutional actors, and there is little evidence of participatory or anti-extractive design beyond transparency and open access.

OPORA demonstrates strong civic participation and advocacy for democratic integrity, but lacks evidence of community ownership/governance or technological sovereignty (no open source/self-hosting), and its anti-extraction orientation is limited by reliance on international donors and traditional organizational structures.

Organise empowers workers to campaign for better conditions and has clear participatory impact, but dossier evidence shows a proprietary, investor-backed platform with no user ownership, self-hosting, or open-source infrastructure, limiting its alignment with deep community governance and technological sovereignty values.

oTree is open-source and self-hostable, but its governance and ownership remain academic rather than genuinely community-driven, its primary users are professional researchers rather than marginalised communities or citizens, and there is no evidence of anti-extraction or participatory justice innovation in its design.

Papertree is open source and supports transparency and climate accountability, but shows no evidence of community governance, direct service to marginalized communities, or participatory democratic structures; its primary users are institutional actors rather than citizens.

Parallel Parliament provides valuable access to parliamentary data for a range of users but lacks community ownership, open-source self-hosting options, or evidence of anti-extractive design, operating instead as a for-profit LLC with a subscription model and no participatory governance.

GOV.UK Pay is a centrally governed, partially open-source payment platform serving government agencies and citizens, but it lacks community ownership, offers limited technological sovereignty, and primarily optimizes state efficiency rather than addressing structural exclusion or wealth concentration.

Plinth is a proprietary, investor-backed platform serving institutional users without community ownership, self-hosting capability, or evidence of anti-extraction innovation, and its design risks reinforce incumbent structures rather than empowering marginalised communities.

PoliMonitor is a for-profit LLC serving professional advocacy and communications users, lacks community ownership, is not open source or self-hostable, and does not demonstrate anti-extraction design, thus scoring low on participatory and justice-oriented criteria despite its utility for advocacy.

Polimorphic is a VC-backed, proprietary SaaS platform serving government agencies with no evidence of community ownership, self-hosting, participatory governance, or structural anti-extraction design, and risks vendor lock-in, thus scoring low on all primary criteria for progressive civic technology.

Prolific is a VC-backed, for-profit platform with no evidence of community ownership, self-hosting, or anti-extraction design; it primarily serves institutional users and reinforces platform dependency, though it has enabled some civic research use cases.

Public Editor is a centralized, for-profit platform with no evidence of community ownership, technological sovereignty, or anti-extraction design, and serves primarily professional users, thus scoring low on core progressive civic criteria.

RightsDD is a proprietary, for-profit compliance platform serving corporate ESG professionals, with no evidence of community governance, self-hosting, structural anti-extraction design, or privacy-by-design principles, thus scoring very low on all progressive civic criteria.

While the platform facilitates knowledge sharing among non-profits and is grant-funded without VC control, it lacks community ownership, technological sovereignty, and structural anti-extraction features, with governance and editorial power retained by CAST rather than the user community.

While ShineYourEye serves participatory democracy and citizen engagement in Nigeria and has a nonprofit foundation governance and grant funding, it does not demonstrate community ownership, self-hosting, or anti-extraction innovation beyond transparency, and lacks evidence of privacy-by-design or participatory governance.

GOV.UK One Login is a centralized, government-run authentication platform with partial open source but no evidence of community governance, limited technological sovereignty for end users, and a design that risks state power concentration without clear participatory or anti-extraction elements.

While the project is open source, grant-funded, and provides open-access educational resources, its governance and ownership remain institutionally held by academic partners rather than genuinely community or user-owned, and there is little evidence of participatory or anti-extractive innovation beyond improving professional skills for public servants.

TheyWorkForYou advances parliamentary transparency and supports participatory democracy but lacks strong evidence of community governance, full technological sovereignty, or explicit anti-extractive design, instead operating as a partially open-source, grant-funded nonprofit with a primarily informational service model.

Tor Project scores highly for enabling technological sovereignty and privacy by design, serving marginalized and at-risk communities globally, though its governance model is more nonprofit than fully community-owned, and evidence of participatory decision-making is limited in the dossier.

Ushahidi demonstrates participatory and open-source values with a focus on empowering communities and supporting marginalized groups, but evidence of direct user/community governance, full technological sovereignty, and explicit anti-extraction design is partial or moderate rather than exemplary.

Watch Duty provides valuable real-time wildfire alerts as a nonprofit powered by volunteers, but lacks community ownership, self-hosting, open source, or anti-extraction innovation, functioning primarily as a centralised service rather than a participatory or sovereignty-enabling civic tool.

Despite its civic engagement tagline, We Live It is a VC-backed, LLC-governed, closed-source SaaS platform with no evidence of community ownership, technological sovereignty, or participatory governance, and its design risks reinforcing incumbent power structures rather than challenging them.

While WhatDoTheyKnow is open source, nonprofit, and supports civic participation via FOI, it lacks true community ownership and participatory governance, and its anti-extraction design is limited by its dependence on existing legal frameworks and organizational oversight.

WhatGov is open source and serves a broad public with civic data for democratic participation, but lacks community ownership, participatory governance, or explicit anti-extraction features, functioning primarily as a nonprofit information platform dependent on foundation governance.

Wikidata demonstrates strong open source and self-hosting credentials, serves a broad public, and is governed as a nonprofit project with some participatory elements, but evidence of direct user/community governance and anti-extraction innovation is moderate rather than exemplary given its reliance on the Wikimedia Foundation and major tech funders.

Worker Info Exchange advances participatory democracy and social justice by empowering workers with access to their employment data and challenging platform power, but lacks clear evidence of community ownership, open source, or full technological sovereignty.

WorkInCharities is a proprietary, for-profit job platform with no evidence of community ownership, self-hostability, or structural anti-extraction design, serving primarily as a traditional employment tool for the nonprofit sector.

WriteToThem meaningfully lowers barriers for citizen contact with representatives, but governance remains centralized under mySociety with no evidence of user/community ownership, partial open source and no clear path to technological sovereignty, and limited evidence of anti-extraction or participatory innovation beyond service provision.

Yoti is a VC-backed, proprietary digital identity platform serving primarily institutional and business users, with no evidence of community governance, self-hosting, or anti-extraction design, and only implied privacy safeguards, thus scoring very low on all progressive civic criteria.

Tracka empowers citizens to monitor public projects and addresses implementation gaps, but lacks evidence of community ownership, open-source self-hosting, or a structural anti-extraction design, limiting its alignment with Gamithra's highest standards for participatory governance and technological sovereignty.

While Your Priorities advances participatory democracy and is partially open source, the dossier provides no evidence of genuine community ownership or user governance, and the primary beneficiaries are governments rather than marginalized communities, limiting its alignment with Gamithra's strongest criteria.
